opus-5.5.text:
I think generalization is really the central promise, and honestly the central question, of bringing machine learning into robotics. For decades, the way we built robots was to engineer them very carefully for one specific setting: a fixed factory cell, known objects, known positions. That works beautifully when the world holds still, but the moment you change the lighting, the object, or the table height, the whole system can break. The hope with learning is that instead of hand-specifying every behavior, the robot picks up structure from data that carries over to situations it has never seen.

But I try to be careful about what we mean by "generalization," because people use the word for very different things. There's generalizing to a new instance of the same object, like a different mug. There's generalizing to a new environment, like a different kitchen. And then there's the much harder kind: generalizing to new tasks, or to new physical interactions where contact, friction, and dynamics matter. The first two are improving quickly, partly because of large pretrained vision and language models. The last one is where I think we're still quite early.

What makes robotics different from language or vision is that the robot's data is grounded in physics and in its own body. You can't just scrape the internet for how it feels to insert a plug or fold a towel. So a big part of the question is: where does the data come from, and what kind of data actually leads to transferable skill? I'm optimistic about combining a few sources: large-scale human teleoperation, simulation, and learning from the robot's own experience, with good inductive biases about the physical world.

So my view is that the promise is real. We're already seeing policies that handle variation we couldn't have engineered by hand. But I'd frame it less as "one model that does everything" and more as a steady widening of the range of situations a robot can handle reliably. Reliability matters a lot here, because a robot that works 80% of the time in a home isn't really useful yet. Closing that gap between impressive demos and dependable behavior is, to me, the real test of whether generalization delivers.

r001.rationale: The response stresses reliable performance and says an 80%-reliable home robot is not yet useful, but it does not argue that attempting many tasks is insufficient when the robot performs none of them well.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The promise of generalization is really the whole bet behind robot learning, so I think it's worth being precise about what we mean by it.

In language and vision, we saw that if you scale data and model size, you get systems that handle inputs they've never seen before, and they get better in ways that are roughly predictable. The hope in robotics is that the same recipe transfers: train a policy on enough diverse demonstrations, across enough scenes, objects, and embodiments, and you get a robot that can walk into a new kitchen and do something useful without being reprogrammed.

I believe in that direction, but I'd separate the promise from where we are. There are a few kinds of generalization, and they're not equally hard. Generalizing across visual variation, like lighting or distractor objects, is mostly solved by better pretrained vision backbones. Generalizing across object instances within a category is getting there. Generalizing to new tasks, new motions, or new physical contact strategies is much harder, because the robot has to actually learn something about dynamics, not just perception. And cross-embodiment generalization, where you move from one robot body to another, is still mostly an open research question, even though the early results are encouraging.

The other thing I'd push on is that robotics doesn't have an internet. Language models got a free trillion tokens of human behavior. For robots, every data point costs money and time, and the distribution of that data is narrow because it was collected in a handful of labs and warehouses. So when people say "we just need to scale," the honest follow-up is: scale what? Teleoperation data, simulation, video of humans, or some mix? My view is the mix is the answer, and the interesting engineering is in how you weight those sources so the policy learns physics from the real data and breadth from the cheaper sources.

So I'd say the promise is real, the trajectory is right, but I'm wary of borrowing the timeline from language models. The thing that actually convinces me is not a demo video. It's a model that fails gracefully in a new environment and gets better with a small amount of additional data. That's what generalization looks like in practice, and we're starting to see it, but we're early.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generalization across tasks and environments, but does not argue that attempting many tasks is insufficient when the robot performs none of them well.

astra-6.text:
I think the promise is that a robot can learn something useful from one set of experiences and carry it into a situation it hasn’t seen before. You shouldn’t have to program every object, every room, every possible interaction separately.

But generalization is a very broad word. If a robot learns to pick up a cup, does it work with a different cup? In a different kitchen? With a different gripper? Those are different kinds of generalization, and success on one doesn’t necessarily imply success on the others.

What makes robotics especially interesting is that the robot can act to resolve uncertainty. If it doesn’t know how something will move, it can probe it, observe what happens, and adjust. So I think the promise is bigger than having a policy that produces the right action immediately. It’s having a system that can use prior experience to learn and recover efficiently in a new situation.

I’m optimistic about that. But I’d want to measure it by how much new setup, data, and human help the robot needs when you take it somewhere unfamiliar. That’s where generalization becomes practically meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses transfer across tasks and situations, but does not argue that attempting many tasks is insufficient when the robot performs none of them well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the promise is that a robot can learn something useful in one setting and carry it into another without us having to engineer every detail again. But generalization has a lot of dimensions. Are we talking about a new object, a new room, a new task, or a different robot? Those are very different challenges.

For me, the exciting question is whether learning more tasks makes the next task easier to learn. If every new situation requires collecting another huge dataset and training from scratch, we haven’t really delivered on that promise.

And in robotics, you have to measure this through interaction. It’s not enough for the robot to recognize what’s happening; it has to act, see the consequences, and recover when something unexpected happens. So I’m optimistic, but I’d want to make the claim very concrete: what changed between training and testing, how much adaptation was allowed, and how reliably did the robot succeed?

r001.rationale: The response questions whether new tasks become easier to learn and emphasizes reliable success, but it does not argue that attempting many tasks is insufficient if the robot performs none of them well.
